newsitem.title: GERMANY: Remainder of Berlin Wall to be rescued from decay.
newsitem.headline: Remainder of Berlin Wall to be rescued from decay.

text.p: Several decaying segments of the Berlin Wall may be saved for posterity by a group of real estate developers, politicians and historians who announced rescue plans on Thursday.

The barricade which divided the city for nearly 30 years until the collapse of communism in 1989 has almost disappeared, torn down and carried away by souvenir hunters and developers. Some sections were given away -- recipients include the Pope, former U.S. president Ronald Reagan and museums.
But the consortium, a loose group of interested parties, hope to maintain some of the last standing fragments as a political symbol and tourist attraction.
One section of the Wall has already been preserved as part of an open-air museum.

Berlin firms Noack and Co. and Future Chemie told a news conference they had pledged financial support to protect the "East Side Gallery" -- a 1.2 km (three quarters of a mile) strip covered in murals, the longest remaining segment -- from destruction by vandals and bad weather.
The Gallery artists returned in September to touch up the works they had painted in the months following the fall of the Wall.

The cash-strapped Berlin city government has found it difficult to locate funds for renovation work on the remaining pieces and has proposed plans to mark the route of the 155 km (96 mile) Wall with a memorial copper strip.
The city has said it will settle for a marker in red paint along one section of the Wall's foundations until it can afford a more lasting symbol.

"People are of course happy that the Wall's time was limited," Matthias Maulzsch, an engineer with the Federal Office for Material Research which is investigating ways to protect the Wall, told reporters.
"But they also recognise that it is important that parts of it stay in the city to keep us from forgetting."

"People come from everywhere to see the Wall and their disappointment is enormous when they see how much of it has disappeared," said Rainer Hildebrandt, director of the Haus am Checkpoint Charlie museum at the former Allied border crossing.
Recognising its value as a magnet for tourists, private Berlin promotions agencies have planned tours of the site of the Wall for American soldiers who guarded the U.S. sector until 1989.
Under the caption "Nostalgic Journeys", Berlin Tourism Marketing hopes to attract 5,000 former GIs next year to Berlin where city tours will include the remains of the Wall.

The desire to destroy the Wall as quickly and completely as possible has left confusion about precisely where it stood. Students from the Berlin Technical University are now studying aerial photos from before 1989 to relocate its exact position.
